utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. For the record all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence only of Mr. Haynes. The Prosecution is represented by Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. The witness is already in the courtroom. Let me first make a statement explaining the reason why we are starting 40 minutes late. The reason is that when we came here just before 9.00 to start the sitting, we were informed that there was a technical problem as a result of which the accused, amongst others, wouldn't have been able to follow the proceedings on the monitor. So it was a technical problem that required some time to get fixed. I'm told that it is now fixed, and therefore we can proceed. Yes. Good morning to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome back. I hope you've had a good rest. Last Friday, we finished with your examination-in-chief and Mr. Zivanovic had just started his cross-examination. Today we will continue with it and then we see who else wishes to cross-examine you. I suspect that almost everyone will. Mr. Zivanovic, good morning to you. You may continue from where you left last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have just a couple of more questions for you. In fact, I'm going to ask you for some clarifications. On Friday, when you last testified here, while you were explaining some differences between what you were saying on Friday and your earlier interviews, you emphasised that you were speaking under oath here. I wanted to ask you if that was the reason why you said here the things that you were sure about, whereas in earlier interviews, you were not under oath and you didn't feel the same obligation as you feel before the Court now.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean specifically when saying that I said something on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On Friday, I asked you about the description of that one person, one of the two that you described, and I asked you specifically about the mustache. That is what I'm talking about, because I relied mainly on that, and I see that you answered on Friday, as I quoted before, "I'm speaking under oath here," et cetera. Does that explain the differences between what you said on Friday and what you said in earlier interviews?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, back then, and today, I still don't know who the people were who had come down there. If I knew, I would say publicly before everyone. I don't want to speculate and I don't want to falsely accuse anyone. All that I can say about those men, I have already said in that description, and I stand behind that. The context in which I mentioned those two names is that after those events, several years later, when I saw certain photographs, my comment was that there was a certain resemblance. Beyond that, I didn't say anything in interviews to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about those names. Maybe you didn't understand me.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You insist on the mustache. I told you that I stand behind the description I gave of the first person, but as far as the second person is concerned, I cannot be sure that he had a mustache.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would that then be your answer to my next question, also seeking clarification of what you said on Friday? You said, "I am not 1 million per cent sure." In our language, it could be understood that you were not a million per cent sure but you are a hundred per cent sure. To avoid any ambiguity, does that mean, when you say that, "I'm not sure a person had a mustache," does it mean you're not sure, you cannot confirm, be it million or 100 per cent?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means I can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. In your interviews, you said that when the convoy arrived carrying those prisoners, you said the convoy consisted of about ten vehicles, mainly buses with one or two trucks. You said in the interviews that approximately a half of the people were unloaded from the vehicles and taken inside the school, whereas the other half spent the night in buses and was driven somewhere else in the morning. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm almost convinced that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Meek, appearing for Colonel Beara, will go next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. How are you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm fine, thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, we have evidence that some witnesses for the OTP, who are coming to testify in this Chamber, in this case, were told to lie by Dragan Obrenovic before they gave their statements to the OTP investigators. And I want to ask you, sir, did you have any conversations with anyone, including Dragan Obrenovic, either before you gave your first statement or before you gave your second statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in touch with Mr. Obrenovic since the day he was arrested. As for the attitude of the OTP towards me, although I had certain misgivings before I came here, I have a good memory of my contacts with the OTP and I think that they were very decent towards me, before and during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, prior to Mr. Obrenovic being arrested, did you speak with him concerning the events around the middle of July, of which you've testified here today and Friday?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never uttered a word about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, besides Mr. Obrenovic, that was on my part an example, did you speak with any other person or persons concerning what you should or should not tell the Office of the Prosecutor, either before the first interview or before the second interview, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only conversation I had on that topic was at the command of the battalion after the commander returned from the field. I believe it was on the 23rd of July, when we familiarised him with the facts concerning our participation in the event, and I have some notes about it in my diary, which is in the possession of the office of the Prosecutor, but they didn't find anything to ask me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, just a little earlier here, you testified that you have good memories of your contact with the OTP and that they were very decent towards you. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you remember the end of your second interview, you seemed a little upset with the OTP and you couldn't understand why it was that they told you to lie if someone contacted you about what you were speaking about and they told you, "Should you -- should anyone contact you, tell them we spoke about 1992," and you couldn't understand why they were telling you to lie. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very end of the interview, indeed, we had a sort of misunderstanding. After the first interview that took place in my home they told me that if someone asks me what we had talked about, I should say we had discussed events from 1992, and I kind of opposed that, saying, "Why would I lie about this?" Because I didn't know what the reason would be, since I didn't participate in events of 1992 in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And so you still stand by your testimony this morning that you have good memories of the OTP interviews and they treated you fairly, even though they told to you lie if someone asked you about what you were speaking about? Is that my understanding, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excepting that misunderstanding and maybe a small misunderstanding about my diary, which I have given them and from which they copied the page that was of interest to them, during proofing a couple of days ago, I asked them if they would return that diary to me, because it was a fond memory of that wartime. Somebody answered that they would not. Setting aside those two misunderstandings, I have really nothing bad to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And speaking of your diary, you made that diary, did you not, in order to remember the events that you went through?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my diary, which was not always up to date, but it contains some significant things, and there are a couple of sentences linked to the event that I'm testifying to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, when you say it's not completely up-to-date, do you mean that it wasn't kept in chronological order insofar as you didn't -- you didn't regularly write the events which you experienced down immediately, or sometimes you did and sometimes you didn't?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times when things were more or less normal, I didn't write anything down. And when I was on duty in my shift, I would enter everything that seemed interesting to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's true, sir, that not only would you write down everything that seemed interesting to you; you also wrote down, as correctly as you remembered, the truth of the events which you experienced. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that is written in that diary is completely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, do you recall writing in your diary, which, for the record, is 65 ter, Prosecution 65 ter number -- I don't have a ter number on it. I've got it as an attachment to the OTP interview dated 10 March 2003, a notebook containing a diary for the year 1991 and handwritten notes. But I have an ERN number; the B/C/S version starts at 0327-1037 to 1143 in my copy from the OTP. The English is 0327-1046 to 1049. Could we bring that up on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just thought I could be a little bit helpful to Mr. Meek. The diary is designated P02814 for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to have the English -- the English be page 4 of 5 with ending number ERN 1049. Alongside that, the B/C/S version would be -- and I have it as 1048, which frankly doesn't seem to line up with what I have that the OTP sent. And -- yes, that would be correct. On the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the screen now. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could you please go back one page on that, first, on the B/C/S, 1047? Then on the left side, if you wouldn't mind, it would actually be the English version would be 1049 ending ERN number. Scroll down, please. No. It's not the correct one. Yes, the page before in the English. I still need one more page forward. I'm sorry, previously to that one on the English. Scroll down, please. Here we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you notice that you have written in this diary -- you have entries on this page, I believe, starting at the 10th day of July 1995, correct? In the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, the top. Yes, sir. I'm just curious about the date. Is that correct? 10th day of July 1995, top, in the diary on that page, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the next entry seems to be the 6th day -- or 20th day of June 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it's possible that after returning from leave at home, I leafed through the logbook of the duty officer at the battalion command, and I took things down that seemed interesting, although it was covering a period of over a month or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And I'm not concerned, I just want the dates. I want to verify that. The next date you went to would have been the 2nd day of June -- 20th day of June 1995, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The next date, yes or no, was the 2nd day of July, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes or no, the next date was the 4th of July 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The next date is the 14th of July 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I believe that on that date, you just wrote that "an order arrived to bring up manpower level to 100 per cent and to form one reserve platoon after the escalation of the conflict in Srebrenica. Our lines are still stable and there are no provocations." That's your entry, correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the next page in B/C/S? For the record, I believe we have to skip almost two pages in the English to page 4 of -- can we just scroll up on the B/C/S portion, please? Thank you. One more page on English, please. There we go. Now, witness, after that, we go on down and -- could you scroll down a little bit so we can see the very top of the B/C/S page? Then we go -- and again, I'll tell you that I believe in the B/C/S version it may be the very next page, which I think it is, you went to the 9th day of August, correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the top part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And then the next day would have been the 19th or the 12th day of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The next date being the 17th of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And after that, the 19th of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then we have the 21st day of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then we go -- then the next date is the 30th day of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Again, all of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then after that we have another notation for the 14th of July, and actually you say on Friday, 14.07 for the 14th day, the Friday, that's your next entry; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not visible on my screen. It should be scrolled up a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise for that. There you go.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And again, for that entry, you put down that on Friday, 14 July, "A group of Muslims was brought to Kula who were captured in Srebrenica where they stayed until 16 July." Am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You note after that a group from Srebrenica returned to the front line on 20th day of July 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You then note that, "the commander returned to the battalion on 23 July. On this date, we had a command meeting and we visited all front lines." Is that correct? That's the end of that entry.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there is anything more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again, not to belabour the point, but you've already testified under oath today that everything you put in there, even though it may be out of order or not being sequential, was true. I am correct on that, am I, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by the accuracy of everything that's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Two further questions and I think I'll be finished, sir. One is, you will agree that nowhere in this diary of yours did you ever, even one time, mention on the 14th day of July of 1995, these two officers who you have testified you observed for the first and last time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered all the questions about that a couple of moments ago and anything I might say in addition would be superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, is it true that the OTP, during your proofing session, did not show you a photo lineup in order for you to identify any individual?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not show me during proofing any photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That leads me to one other question, sir. I just want to confirm on Friday, upon questioning by the honourable Judge Agius, you indicated that you had never been shown any photographs by the Office of the Prosecutor during your interviews, and I'm going to add any other time off the record on those interviews or any time. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Prosecutor's Office never showed me any photos whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Meek. I have on my list the Nikolic Defence team. Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions. First of all, I would like you to clarify one thing for me, and that is your position in the battalion of the brigade. You were the assistant for intelligence duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Zvornik Brigade had a separation between security and intelligence and that one person was the assistant Chief of Staff for intelligence and the other person was the assistant for security?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That body was a joint body at times and at times it was a separate body. I can't be more precise and tell you more precisely when these things occurred in what form.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I told you that in July 1995, Dusko Vukotic was the assistant Chief of Staff for intelligence, and Drago Nikolic the assistant Chief of Staff for security, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Vukotic and there is no reason for me not to believe you that that body was split into two parts at that particular moment in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Then next thing I would like to ask you to confirm for me is this: I would like to go back to the three days in July 1995, in the school and around the school in Pilica. On the 14th, 15th and 16th of July if I understood you well, the way you understood the situation and the efforts to preserve peace and quiet in the village during those days up to the morning of the 16th of July, my impression that arises from the -- your testimony was that your view was that these prisoners would be exchanged on any of these three days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This lingered in the air from the moment they arrived. One of the possibilities that remained until their very departure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And as far as I could understand, you and the other soldiers from the battalion were afraid as to what this group of prisoners might do and how they might affect the security and safety in the village. You feared for your family and friends, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were afraid that the situation in the school would escalate but we were also afraid of some people who might arrive from the neighbouring shops, drunk and so on and so forth. At any given moment, an incident might have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were you afraid of what the prisoners might have done as a group if they had left the school building?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to discuss the soldiers who escorted the prisoners. On page 11385, on Friday, you explained that they were arrogant, these soldiers, who escorted the prisoners and my conclusion from all that were that you and your colleague from the battalion were absolutely powerless when it came to the actions of these soldiers who escorted the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the school, there were some troops from the 1st Battalion but not for a single moment and not for any way could they influence the overall developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could they have influenced the behaviour of the escorts?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. To be honest, I would rather say that they were afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On Friday, on pages 1409 and 1410 [as interpreted]. My learned friend from the Prosecution asked you on several occasions about the potential incidents and bodies, whether they existed, whether the incidents happened between the 14th and 16th of July around the school, and your answer was negative to every such question. What I would like to ask you now is this: Would you exclude the possibility that in your absence any of these soldiers did create an incident or maybe even killed a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I did not see any torture, I did not see any killing committed by these other soldiers. I didn't see any of that, and nothing of the sort was conveyed to me by my colleagues from the battalion. The gentleman from the OTP asked me whether I had seen some bodies on the road that I took every day. I claim that there were no bodies whatsoever. Then he mentioned certain streams or brooks. I did not cross any streams. My concern were the soldiers of the 1st Battalion and the population, the local population, and nothing but that. Whatever bad happened to these prisoners, either around the school or elsewhere, happened at the hands of the soldiers that I didn't know. I claim with full responsibility that not a single soldier from the 1st Battalion did anything bad around the school, in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is exactly the way I understood you, sir. That's why I would like to ask you this: If something bad happened with those soldiers have reported to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they would have told me, but I also told you what I think about the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the three days of the events in Pilica and around Pilica, you would come and then you would return. You knew Drago Nikolic. Did you see him or did you speak to him on any other occasion, save for that one telephone conversation that you had on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Save for that one telephone conversation, I never either saw him or spoke to him. I claim with full responsibility that at the time when I was at the school, none of the officers from the Zvornik Brigade visited the school in Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday, on pages between 11395 and 11397, you testified about your visit to the command of the Zvornik Brigade on the 15th of July 1995. In the office of the duty operative officer you met up with four or five officers and you explained what had happened at the time, i.e., that you did not feel that they understood you. My question is this: Did you have an impression that the officers from the Zvornik Brigade could influence that situation in Pilica or were they just observers and nothing more?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My battalion was the furthest from the command of the Zvornik Brigade. It was about 40 kilometres away from the command of the Zvornik Brigade. In normal times when anybody of us from the command arrived with a certain task it was a normal thing for the duty officer to drop everything and to solve the problem for which we had come to visit in order to allow us to return to our unit as soon as possible. You will agree with me that this was not just an ordinary problem because the problem of prisoners of war demanded a different treatment. Their lack of interest for that situation showed me that this is some -- this was something that they were not involved in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this: While you were at the staff of the Zvornik Brigade, and when you were talking to these people, did you meet up with Mr. Drago Nikolic at the time? Did you see him? Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't want to go to see Mr. Nikolic because I knew that he could not do anything about this whole issue. The duty officer at the brigade command is a person who stands in for the brigade commander in his absence and he is the one who can make certain decisions, and that is the only reason why I went to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question, please, about the conversation and communication that you had with the officers in the duty officer's office, when one of them approached you with certain comments. Did anybody tell you at the time that you should kill those prisoners in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I've already said that this was an informal conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And did you see that conversation as a way to instruct you to commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you returned to Pilica, you didn't do anything bad to the prisoners, either you or your colleagues from the battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. The Borovcanin team asking to cross-examine the witness for about 15 minutes. Mr. Stojanovic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to look at some documents with you and ask for some clarifications of the contents of these documents. Can we please look at P1807, the Prosecutor's document, P1807. This is an aerial view of the Pilica hall and the road next to it. Sir, you will see in front of you on the screen in a minute. While this is being done and while we are waiting for this photo, I would like to ask you this: There was a check-point of the civilian police in Pilica, in the course of the war? Sir, can you find your bearings in this photo? And I would kindly ask the usher to help us with marking the photo. Sir, do you see the culture hall in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please encircle it and above the circle, can you put letters DK, standing for culture hall?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that during the war, in this area, there was a check-point of the civilian police used to control traffic and movement of goods and people and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but I can't be sure whether it was there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This photo, does it show the place where that check-point was when it existed in the area? Can you see that place in this photo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I can help you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the tasks were of the civilian police when they manned that check-point?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I was a soldier, and the area of responsibility of my battalion involved the area from Medici to Crne Stijene, about three kilometres in depth. Whatever was beyond the three kilometres was under the authority of the civilian bodies of authority. And this included the police, so I would rather not tell you anything about the way they worked and what they did and how they did whatever they were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, were they anywhere in the area that is depicted in the photo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really would not want to speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask you to put today's date, which is 14 May 2007, in the upper right-hand corner, and could you also sign this photo?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Just one sentence, if you will allow me. When I returned from the brigade on the 15th, I would like to show you where I stopped for maybe two minutes from which place I took a look towards the culture hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead and mark that place with a cross.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you put the date 15 July next to that cross?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Do you need the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, 1995.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is all about this document. Thank you, Madam Usher. Sir, could we now look at P2814, which is your diary? I would like to thank the usher. We won't need her assistance any more, I believe. Can we look at page 3 of the English version, or the last paragraph on page 11 of the B/C/S version, which is page 1047. Could we please look at the last paragraph? Very well. This is it. Thank you. Can we also place the English version next to the B/C/S version? Sir, before our first break, just one question. It says here n the last sentence, "the losses are still not final." Can you see that, sir? "The losses are not final. The police had six dead, the Legend had three. The blue police a few, and also the battalion." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've not been able to locate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the fourth line from the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've been able to find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here, "the losses are still not final." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you come by this information about the number of people who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the most topical thing at the time was major fighting that was going on in the vicinity of the brigade command, and this is information that arrived from every day fighting, from the conversations between Mr. Pandurevic and the Muslim commander whose name I believe was Semso Muminovic, and the topic was opening the corridor and the passage of that column towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say Legenda had three men killed. Who do you mean there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean a special unit called the Drina Wolves. Whether he was with them or with some other men, I don't know, but I suppose that he was with his own soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mean the blue police had several mean dead, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, when you say the police had six men dead, do you mean the special brigade of the police which was at Baljkovica that day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find that. I'm not sure if I meant the civilian police, but probably I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 16th of July, part of the Special Police Brigade was involved in combat at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you think that you might be speaking precisely about the losses of that Special Police Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I cannot be emphatic about that. MR. STOJANOVIC [Interpretation] Maybe this is a good time for a break, Your Honour, because I'll have two more documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, before the break we were looking at your diary and the number of losses you recorded. During the break, after consulting with our client, and also the Prosecution documentation, 65 ter, I just wanted to ask you, since you allowed the possibility, is it possible that the six policemen you recorded as dead were perhaps members of the military police of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible that I meant the military police, because the very next line says, "Blue police, several."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly why we wanted this clarified. And we also obtained the names of those men who are unfortunately dead. Let me ask you: Do you know a man called Pero Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do. It's a man who used to be president of the local community. He used to be also sometimes engaged in our battalion and sometimes he was relieved of military duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, and do you remember, whether maybe he went with you when you went to visit the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly didn't go with me. He may have gone on his own initiative and on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. I have the Miletic Defence team. Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Madam Fauveau. And the Gvero team had indicated that they do not wish to cross-examine this witness. Is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's not changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that leaves us only with the Pandurevic Defence team. Mr. Sarapa, you had asked for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could we see on the screen 7D493? Could we just downsize it a bit? This is good. This is a section of a map that shows the area of Pilica and the surrounding area. The markings RTI, 34, and RTD 1 at the bottom mean nothing to us. I just showed the map to the witness so that he could draw in certain positions.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot draw anything on this map. If you can enlarge it a bit, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could we accommodate the witness and enlarge it, please? That's too much. This is all right. Leave it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may be all right for you, Mr. Sarapa, but I very much doubt it's going to be all right for the witness. It's not all right for me. I can barely see a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think some things are visible. We'll see if the witness will be able to show us. I think it's legible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous image was clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: All right now? Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you please, the usher will give you something to use as a pen. Can you draw, please, the lines of defence of your battalion, the way they were in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here on the right-hand side we were at the boundary of Tursanovo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can you draw a line?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is our separation with the East Bosnian Corps. Our line went from Medici, the Dzamija road, Popova Kosa, and ended with Crne Stijene.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now could you show us on this map where was your command post?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the balloon was in a house in Manojlovici village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I don't know if we can see it on the map. Could you mark next to the line you drew LO, which means "linija odbrane," defence line, and place a K next to Manojlovici?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you see Teocak village here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you use another colour for Teocak?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Whose forces were next to Teocak? Who populated the village in majority?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim forces were there ahead of our forward defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could you show us Rastosnica and Laze villages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can see them on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Look below Teocak.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Rastosnica is here. [Marks]. And Laze --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Look a bit further up. Do you know that these villages were burned down, the Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the population was expelled. There was no more Serb population there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Next to Laze and Rastosnica, would you please the letters SST, which would stand for, "burned down Serb villages"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And next to Teocak, please MS.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can you find Kula on the map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here is the school at Kula. The same colour?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No. Use another colour and make a little --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please get closer to the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And the letter, "sh," s with a diacritic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you've marked this, could you just place your initials at the bottom in the right corner on the map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And today's date.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could we just move the map a little to the left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it that you haven't finished with this map as yet? Because we were about to store it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I would just like to see whether it's possible to write --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Make a little cross next to Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see Branjevo on this map. You don't need to move it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And now, use the red pen to write after this RTD 1, "1 PB," the 1st Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. We can store this now. Could we now see 7D155? You have already told us that in July 1995 you had an insufficient number of soldiers in trenches.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that in my diary, where I gave the example of three or four different groups that were in the field at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now, look at this document. Could we raise it a bit so we can see the bottom line?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now, look at this. It says, "1st Infantry Battalion, 25 soldiers, 1100 hours, to be sent to Kamenica. Djevanje Rijeka settlement." It says at the top, "Act on Obrenovic's instructions." Tell me, do you agree that this entry about sending 25 soldiers to the area of Kamenica, 25 soldiers from the 1st Battalion, this was done on the orders of Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that alongside the group that went to Srebrenica, at some point they asked for another 25 soldiers to make ambushes somewhere in that area, but I cannot be certain whether we actually sent them, because of the problems I've already mentioned. I'm more inclined to think that this group that was in Srebrenica returned to Zvornik on the 15th, I believe, and was kept for a day or two in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Would you agree that it is not that group, because this entry dates back to the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that they requested these men, but I'm not sure that we were able to send them this number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could we now see document P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, did you tell us what this document is about? Whose writing is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a working notebook of the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see document P2814? That is the witness's diary. And could we have page ERN number 03271047? Could you scroll it up a bit so we can see the second half of the page? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now, counting from the bottom, line 15, where it says, "Around the 15th of July, one platoon went to set up an ambush near Kamenica and stayed there for three days." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, and it's probably the answer to your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So could we agree that that was the platoon that executed the order of Dragan Obrenovic to send those men?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Could we now see document 7D159, also a working notebook. We can read here, look at the top of the page, "TG, from Pelemis. There are problems with personnel." You can see that, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Do you agree that the said entry relates to the problems you had in raising those 25 men that Obrenovic requested from your battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've spoken about this more than once. That's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So your answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can you tell me, do you know who Dusan Jokic is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Never mind, then. Did you hear that at that time, in July, related to the Srebrenica events, Commander Pandurevic ever issued an order that no prisoners should be taken, that all prisoners should be killed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, absolutely never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Since you were assistant commander of that battalion for security, do you believe that such an order, had it ever been issued, would have come to your notice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The commander of the brigade would send that order down his own chain of command, and in addition, I would receive information about that problem from Mr. Nikolic, down another line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Next to the school in Kula, did you see Radivoje Lakic during those days?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. That man was seriously ill, an agronomist by training, and he was assigned to another job. He had no business there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Can you see -- did you see Jevto Bogdanovic near that school?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that I didn't see him during the period I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you. Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Is there re-examination, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As long as we have what we have on the screen in EDS and -- in e-court, I'm sorry. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I call up P377, please, in e-court? Okay. I'd like to go to page 142 of the B/C/S version, which should be the same as the page that was previously on the screen, and page 23 of the English version, if we could have that up, please. Okay. Can we scroll down just a little bit? All right. Can we try paging forward one page, please? Okay. Now I think we can scroll down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to locate the English translation of the document that my learned friend, Mr. Sarapa, just used a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We had it before on a split screen, so what's the problem? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We can proceed with this one, I guess. I think it's page 24 is the English translation of this document and we'll see if we can work on the other one after. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see this on the screen, Witness, this document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could just refer your attention to the entries made in relation to the 1st Battalion, do you see an entry relating to the 50 litres of oil and 20 litres of gasoline for the transport of troops to Kula? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you also see an entry relating to ten crates of 7.62-millimetre ammunition, relating to the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of whether or not those entries were made in respect to the activities of your battalion at the school on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I'm the right person to answer this question; however, I can give you a sentence or two. Since I was at the school, it is certain that I did not ask for anything myself. As for the deputy commander who was in the battalion command, I can't speak for him. But there is a possibility that one of the people who were not there asked for those things and that the duty operative officer entered the request, as the request coming from the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned previously, with respect to 7D159, which was, I believe, an entry of the duty officer logbook that was shown to you, it was shown to you by my learned friend, Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Vanderpuye, can you confirm the date of this entry in this logbook? Can you see it somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. If we could scroll up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have to go to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, this was on the 16th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Can you confirm that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can't, and I would like to see it -- I would like to have it on the screen so that we can all see it. I would just like to locate the page if I may have just one moment. Okay. I think we can find it on page 16 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to go back eight pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's page 135 of the B/C/S version. I believe we do have the date displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you see that, Witness, the date of the entry relating to the question I just put to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you just state for the record what that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we have to make sure there is no change of date between page 16 and 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice two things, Mr. Sarapa on his feet. Let's start with -- yes, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to the date, we are eight pages back. We have to make sure that this is the date in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what we are trying to do. The only thing is that I had understood Ms. Nikolic's contribution to indicate that the date was the 16th, while here it looks as if it is the 15th. So if anyone can help us see clearer, I think it --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think if we can go forward, we can establish the date from which the 16th entries occur, and I understand we'll find that ten pages in advance of the page we are currently on. So we've gone eight pages back, we'll go ten pages forward, and we should find the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's, to be doubly sure, go page by page. I mean, it's not time wasted, definitely. Okay, go ahead. All right. Go ahead. Okay. Go ahead. This is where we were when we first started. Go ahead. Yeah, and we come to the 16th on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I hope that satisfies my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, do you agree it's the 15th that we are talking about? According to the diary, any way. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the entry on the previous page, you can see that the first entry is on the 16th at 6.00. So it is very difficult to say whether the time before midnight or after midnight was entered as the 16th here, because you see here that this entry was made at 6.00 in the morning so it's very difficult to define the time. But if we want to be very formalistic, it may well be the morning of the 16th. I will allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I got your point. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to point out that your comment on line 17 of page 32, you indicated that according to the diary, any way, and I don't believe this was a diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, point made by Ms. Nikolic is that if the entry referred to any time past midnight, it would still come under the 16th even though it shows up before the first entry for the 16th. So this is basically when she is saying and I'm not going to comment on that, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We do plan to elicit further testimony on this specific issue. Just for the record, though, I think it's fair to say that the entry to which the witness's attention was directed precedes the date as indicated in the logbook of the 16th of July and falls within the time frame of the dates, the 15th and the 16th. Just so that we are in agreement, I think, on the record as to what's contained in the logbook entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he's up again. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to emphasise once again that before the 16th, here we have an entry that was made at 6.00, 6.30, all after midnight, 6.35. And finally the 16th of July. And even where it says the 16th of July, the first entry is at 7.20. On the 15th, we have entries for the events that happened, as it arises from what is on the screen, not on the 15th but on the 16th, at 0600 and 0630. This is after midnight, which means that these things happened on the 16th of July. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Sarapa. I don't think there is going to be agreement between the two sides so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated earlier upon some questioning by my learned friend, Mr. Sarapa, that there was an entry, 7D159, if I could have that displayed on e-court? So the English translation, I think, is on page 13, and the B/C/S is at 132. You had indicated, upon questioning about this document, that there was some indication that there was some difficulty getting people together, troops together, from the 1st Battalion. And that was to go to participate in ambushes. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, is that a specific entry in this logbook?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer your question. I'm not clear what you want from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, did you see that particular entry relating to the difficulty in rounding up men to go to participate in ambushes in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean what it says here in the upper part of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Do you see in there a specific reference to difficulty with personnel as concerns the participation of those personnel in ambushes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I've spoken about that on several occasions, and that there is no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, was it the case that there was difficulty rounding up men from the 1st Battalion to go and guard or provide security for the school at Kula?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've already spoken about the problems that prevailed in the 1st Battalion at the moment when the battalion commander was not there. I have to tell you that my commander was a courageous and brave man. He went everywhere, wherever actions were taking place. From Banja Luka to Sarajevo, he would be there, and whenever he left the brigade commander during that time was supposed to send an officer either because he knew that there were a lot of problems there. On one occasion it was Milan Martic who died a few days ago. On another occasion, it was Mihajlo Galic. On a third occasion it was Dusko Vukotic. And this repeated on several occasions, which means, pursuant to the orders of a superior command, you do things, you don't ponder upon things. If my commander had been in the unit, he would have displayed his authority. When he received an order from the brigade commander on two or three occasions, he telephoned the brigade commander to explain to him that our unit was not capable of performing the task, and then the brigade commander would assign that task to another unit. I repeat: Unfortunately, during this particular period of time relevant to my testimony, the battalion commander was not present in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps my question was rather inartfully phrased so let me try it a different way. What I want to know is whether or not this entry that you see in front of you, whether or not that entry relates to the provision of men for the purpose of ambushes or the provision of men as relates to providing security for the school, if you can tell that from this specific entry.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise answer as to what this referred to exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've testified on cross-examination in response to some questions put to you by my learned friend Ms. Nikolic, about the ability of you and your men to take action with respect to what was going on at the school. Now, with respect to that, my first question is: What effort did you make to do anything about what was going on at the school, if any?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic? And Mr. Sarapa? Ms. Nikolic first.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, within the scope of my cross-examination, I have never put any question to the witness about the actions that were undertaken with regard to the events in the school and around the school. My questions were relative to the relationship between the battalion troops and the troops that escorted the prisoners, and the Prosecutor has already put enough questions about this specific subject and has already received the answers that they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to join my learned friend Nikolic and I would like to add that on several occasions, the witness has already said it that they couldn't do anything. I will paraphrase him by saying that they were just the silent observers of everything that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would also join on that. It's asked and answered and outside the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, in line 20, I think we need to make a small adjustment to indicate that it's Mr. Sarapa because he started speaking before Ms. Nikolic had even finished saying -- finished her statement. So, now you have three guns pointing at you, Mr. Vanderpuye. What's your position? It's been suggested that you have more or less built on a premise -- built your question on a premise that is incorrect or does not reflect the line of questions that Ms. Nikolic had put to the witness and which he had answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to the submissions of my learned friends, I think on several occasions during the examination that was conducted by Ms. Nikolic, the witness indicated that -- he even went so far as to suggest that his men were afraid of the -- the other soldiers that were there, that they were afraid of the prisoners, and to that extent, in addition to the soldiers that were there, and my question is to ascertain -- and that's the reason -- let me just rephrase it. That they were afraid of these soldiers that were there, that they had no ability to control the events as they unfolded there, and that that's the reason why they didn't take any action with respect to what was going on there. So my question is specifically put to that issue, which is what actions, if any, they had -- they did undertake. And I think it's responsive -- I think it's responsive to the issues that were developed on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sarapa? Mr. Sarapa first and Ms. Nikolic afterwards. Yes, Mr. Sarapa, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this question shouldn't be put because the witness has belaboured on the point of what had been done. He went to the brigade command for a specific reason which was to deal with the problems, to ask for assistance. In other words, he has answered that question already, more than once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to go back to the question that my learned friend has put to the witness on page 37, lines from 19 to 23. And in conclusion, my learned friend says that because of the entire situation, the troops of the 1st Battalion could not control the situation because they feared both the escorts and the prisoners and they did not take any actions. If the witness stated then, that, then I'm really not clear why my learned friend is now putting the question to the witness as to what actions were undertaken since the witness has stated clearly that they didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think the specific question that was put by my learned friend was on -- it's on page 14, looks like line 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, I mean but any way, let's conclude on this. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, page 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Line 14, the question was what I would like -- with respect to the answers that the witness had given concerning the conduct of his men or inability to act, my learned friend asked specifically, "What I would like to ask you now is this: Would you exclude the possibility that in your absence any of these soldiers did create an incident or maybe even killed a prisoner?" And the answer to that question was a rather long answer but it didn't effectively answer the question, essentially said that he did not observe any torture or any killing that was committed by these other soldiers. I think that my question is relevant because the witness has testified that they didn't engage in any action, he was specifically asked whether or not he could exclude the possibility that in fact they did, and that's the reason why I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this point has already been covered, Mr. Vanderpuye. Please move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the capacity in which you were acting at the time while you were at the school, if you had become aware of information regarding the mistreatment or killing of prisoners, did you have the authority or the ability or responsibility to arrest or intercede or act to prevent that -- prevent that from occurring?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I was very precise when I spoke about the events that took place around the school. There is no doubt, and I repeat that there were a few soldiers from the 1st Battalion there. And I repeat, not for a moment, not in any way could we have influenced the developments. The people who were there, whom I didn't know, could, at any point, do whatever they wanted and that would be my answer to your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I noticed you at one point standing, Mr. Sarapa, but the witness had already started --

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the answer I've just heard, there is no point in me raising any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question, Mr. Vanderpuye? What are you waiting for?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just rereading his answer to make sure I don't repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You made no effort to arrest anybody based on what you knew and what you observed; is that reasonable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic? One moment before you answer the question. Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Sarapa. Ms. Nikolic first.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, asked and answered. Second, this is a leading question. The witness already explained everything in his own words. I believe this question is superfluous and is leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I join in what Mrs. Nikolic said. That's precisely what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You indicated earlier in your testimony that part of your responsibility or duties as an assistant commander for security, intelligence, was to report to the battalion commander deficiencies that you observed or misconduct. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this goes beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it's a question that is being put as a prelude for the next question. So we have to hear the next question. First he answers yes or no and then we hear the next question, and probably we'll find more objections and then we decide. Yes, Witness, you need to answer this question. You are being asked if it is correct that earlier on in your testimony, you stated that part of your responsibility or duties as an assistant commander for security, intelligence, was to report to the battalion commander deficiencies that you observed or misconduct. Do you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly, when I was answering the question concerning my duties and responsibilities, I did say that, but I'll repeat: 95 per cent of my activities boiled down to daily inspections of the forward defence line, reporting to the commander about any deficiencies I noticed, in order for the commander to be able to take steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your next question, Mr. Vanderpuye? Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have that responsibility with respect to what you observed or knew about during the time that you were at the school?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, did you still have that responsibility to report to the battalion commander deficiencies that you observed while during the time that you were at the school? Did you still carry those responsibilities with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said that the battalion's zone of responsibility was as I described it. Anything outside that area of responsibility fell within the purview of civilian authorities. And the school was located in an area beyond our zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, with the resources that you had that were available to you at the school -- with the resources that were available at the battalion, were those sufficient to control the situation at the school?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. We were not instructed to check or control anything around the school. But let me emphasise again: Our troops had no combat experience whatsoever. Persons who had any experience had been sent to three or four locations on the front line. The rest that remained with the battalion was practically unusable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With the Chamber's leave, I have just one question that arises from the cross-examination of my colleague, Mr. Sarapa, page 28, lines 8 to 17. It concerns the order of Commander Pandurevic that was never carried out. So lines 8 to 17, but especially 15 to 17 with references to Mr. Nikolic on page 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have our permission to proceed, Ms. Nikolic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Witness, that will hopefully clarify your answer to my colleague Mr. Sarapa. When he asked you whether you remembered whether Commander Pandurevic ever issued an order, meaning that the prisoners should be killed, back in July, you said no, such an order was never issued or sent down, and you also said that, had it been, you would have heard about it from Drago Nikolic down another chain of command. My question is whether you had ever received such information from Drago Nikolic along the lines of my colleague's question, namely that prisoners should be killed.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. My only contact with Mr. Nikolic was that telephone call on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No information, that means no order to you or your battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO PERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, yes, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another follow-up question from the redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Follow up question following what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Prosecutor's question concerning the people at the school, if you would allow me just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We are not going to allow you, neither one nor more questions, Mr. Sarapa. We need to move. It's not the practice that we continue as if it's a ping pong game because next thing, Mr. Vanderpuye will want more questions and we'll continue like that. So witness, we don't have any further questions for you, which means that your testimony ends here. You've been very patient with us. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony, and I also on behalf of everyone wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for those good wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just noticed one mistake in the transcript. It's page 43, line 14. I really am not sure that I said "down another chain of command." I meant down another line. I -- I'll try to have this error removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, you were referring to page 28. So whatever is there is -- but point taken. You don't need to worry about this, Ms. Nikolic. So now, documents, Mr. Vanderpuye? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have only P02814, which at this point we would offer in its entirety since extensive use was made of it on cross-examination. I think it would be appropriate to put the entries in context in light of the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections to that? We hear -- yes, spoke too soon. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, can my colleague just confirm what are the dates that are enclosed in that full document and whether we have a full translation for all of these dates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good point. Good point. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye? I suppose you need a little bit of time to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, the Borovcanin Defence team wishes to tender the photo that was marked by the witness, and it will be given 4D IC 00108. Any objections? I suppose none. So that document is being so admitted. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no objections.
