utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, is Mr. Vanderpuye requesting the diary -- this witness's diary be put in evidence? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's according to what I read here, is attachment A to OTP's interview statement dated the 10th March. That is a notebook containing a diary calendar for the year 1991 and handwritten notes, particularly 03271047 to 1048. This is what I have. Now, if this has been updated -- if this has been updated, what certainly has been updated is that it seems that he wishes to tender the entire notebook because he said that a lot of reference was been made to this document. So I think I am still awaiting -- we are still awaiting for his answer to Mr. Bourgon's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know as much as you know on this. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. From what we have been able to ascertain, the diary contains entries from 28th February 1995 through October 10 -- through January 10, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and what are you seeking to admit? I mean this is what Mr. Bourgon basically wants to know, and Mr. Meek, and I suppose everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We are seeking to admit the book itself, the physical document that contains the entries that have been referred to in -- both by the Prosecution and the Defence. It's a physical -- it's the physical book itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection to that? Obviously -- yes, Ms. Nikolic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour -- I'm sorry, Ms. Nikolic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the book has not been translated. Only five or six pages have been translated, the ones that were used in court today either by the Prosecution or in cross-examination. So the Defence would not object to the pages that have been translated and have been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, just to have a final clarification, you have only - and others - only made use of these five pages from the entire book, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So why should we have the rest if it hasn't been made use of?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think also it puts it in context, because some questions were put to the witness about the order in which the entries were made themselves. I don't know whether or not it can be generalised to the entire document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will admit these five pages only. If at any later point in time you need to make further reference to this book and you wish to tender it, we'll deal with that at the time. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I'm putting Mr. Vanderpuye in a bad spot. As you can see we are talking to him and giving him advice. We merely have asked that to be in evidence because, as you know, there is a reburial operation, September, October. I would have thought the Court, the Defence, would want to look at those entries. There is nothing in those entries that we see, but if anyone is curious about that, I think it's relevant. That's why. But if -- we are fine with the pages you have but that's -- that's why. We don't want to bring this fellow back to have him talk about those things. But there is nothing in there so we are fine with the ruling but that's the only reason why we offered the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. No. We stay with the five pages, Mr. McCloskey, and Mr. Vanderpuye. Saving what I stated earlier, that if there is a future need to come, to revisit this document in its entirety we'll do that but not at the time being. Is there any other Defence team that wishes to tender any documents? Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Meek? Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to tender 7D155, just one page of the working notebook, with an English translation provided. Then 7D159, another page of the same notebook with an English translation. And 7D493, the map marked by the witness today. That's my third document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from anyone? Prosecution and other Defence teams? Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is whether P377 has been admitted already or not in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My understanding is that it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the entire book has been admitted already, what is the point of admitting one page of it separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was just going to respond to Judge Kwon's question. I don't think there is a special need to admit the page over and above the document that's already in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you and with Judge Kwon. On certain instances we have done that. We have allowed that, though it was the exception rather than the rule basically. So I wouldn't break Mr. Sarapa's heart, if he is so keen on having these pages, two pages, admitted into evidence separately. If you're not too keen, then you may withdraw your request and we'll leave it at that. Yes, Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not insisting, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then if you're not insisting, I think we drop them and we stick to P -- exactly, the marked map, 7D493, if I am not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 7D IC 109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. That brings us to -- yes, Mr. Bourgon? Always on the same witness, Mr. Bourgon or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's just an observation concerning the last decision of the Trial Chamber to admit those five pages of this document. I note for the record, Mr. President, that this document was not on the Rule 65 ter list for the Prosecution. If they are going to use any such documents, they should seek leave to have this document added to the Rule 65 ter list before they do so. And the status of this document being a diary, I mean, we have a statement that was given to us or an interview. This was an annex to the interview but there was no number. And this document should not be admitted unless they first ask for the document to be added to the list. And then we -- then we are on notice that this is a document that may be -- may be filed into evidence. Now, the Trial Chamber has rendered a decision, and we have no problem with the decision, but the Prosecution must comply with Rule 65 ter in the future. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I apologise. Was the interview statement itself, the 10th March 2003, included in the 65 ter list or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. So, I mean, I just want to make sure that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, it was not but I would also just point out for my learned friend that the diary was essentially made use of on cross-examination in this case, to the extent that there was any examination on the diary itself that I can recall that I did, it would have been on redirect and I don't believe that I did. So the only -- so the only use that's been made of the document itself has been by the Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's true, Mr. Vanderpuye, but it's also true that you had indicated it in -- as your exhibit or the sole exhibit that you had in mind to tender in connection with this witness. So I think we can leave it at that. Point taken, Mr. Bourgon, and I'm sure this is not the last time that we have encountered this problem but let's do our utmost to try and limit cases or eliminate them if possible. So are we ready to bring in the next witness? Yes, we can have the break now, if you wish to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was about to make that suggestion. I think it will make life easier for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, so we will have a 25-minute break starting from now. Basically we'll start again just before quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to address the Chamber before we usher in the next witness or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No preliminaries, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And no preliminaries on the part of the Defence either? Just putting a simple question: Is it also one of those cases where we should alert the witness to Rule 90(E) or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not in this case, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so but since the information that we have at our disposal, which is in any case very scanty, I'm never really in a position to know. All right. So where is Madam Usher? She went to fetch the witness, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning or good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to welcome you to this courtroom. You're about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you're kindly asked to enter the solemn declaration -- make a solemn declaration that is required by our Rules. The text is being handed to you now and that is tantamount to a solemn undertaking that you will be testifying the truth. Go ahead, read it out aloud and then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Thayer will be putting some questions to you, and he will then be followed by the various Defence teams on cross-examination. I don't know if we'll finish today, most likely not, but Mr. Thayer you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Milanko Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber where you were born and raised, please?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 26th of January, 1948, in Zivaljane [as interpreted] village in Rogatica municipality. I was raised in Rogatica, and since -- between 1962 and 1992 I resided in Gorazde. From 1993 -- actually, since 1993, I've lived in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, you identify yourself as a Bosnian Serb by ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just briefly tell the Trial Chamber what is your educational background, please?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I completed grammar school in Gorazde, the school of electrical engineering in Sarajevo, I have a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you've been primarily employed in the field of telecommunications; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Since 1980, I've been employed in telecommunications, until this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'd like to do briefly is just to review with you your military service history. And if anything I summarise is incorrect or needs elaboration, please feel free to do so. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were mobilised into the VRS in December of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: From that time until the end of June 1995, you served in the Zvornik Brigade as chief of communications?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at sometime at the end of June 1995, you were demobilised. Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, just briefly why you were demobilised?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I was demobilised because a professional officer was appointed as chief of communications, and by this, my post was discontinued, because I was a civilian. I had not served in the army, but since I was an expert in telecommunications, I had been appointed as chief of communications and I indeed served as chief of communications during that particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And approximately two weeks later, you were mobilised again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you were mobilised again in early July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Because the chief of communications was supposed to go on duty with the brigade, so I was temporarily engaged in order to cover for the functioning of communications in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was that particularly -- particular duty or operation, sir, that called the chief of communications away?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: It was the operation involving Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the time period after you were brought back in early July of 1995, can you tell the Trial Chamber what your position was?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I acted as chief of communications in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this period of time, did you also, from time to time, serve in another capacity within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I was also assistant duty operative officer of the time. That was my assignment from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you hold a rank in either position, that is the chief of communications or in your role as assistant to the operations duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I did not have a rank. I was a foot soldier. I did not have a military rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's correct, sir, that you served until approximately December of 1995, basically through the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you were chief of communications, prior to being demobilised, who was your direct superior?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic, who was the chief of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say chief, are you referring to Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Chief of Staff of the brigade, Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were remobilised in early July, who was your direct superior at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Obrenovic was commander, but, again, he was my direct superior because he acted in both positions, so I was again subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were serving as chief of communications, did you work out of a particular office?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I had an office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where was it located?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Across the corridor from the office of the operations duty officer. Not directly across but somewhat to the side but in the same corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is this at the Standard barracks of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, was the office on the ground floor or on the first floor, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: On the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this might be a little obvious but when you were working as the assistant to the duty officer, did you work in a particular office at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I worked from the office of the duty officer. A duty officer has to sit in the office dedicated to the duty officer and he must not move. He must not leave that office while he's on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions about the general role and responsibility of the duty officer in a moment, sir, but while we are talking about the actual office can you please just describe how the operations duty officer office was set up? What type of equipment was in it?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: There was a telephone, a land line, civilian land line telephone. There was also a telephone used for extension. And there was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last type of telephone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters didn't catch up what you said about the type of telephone. The answer, what we have is, "There was -- there was a telephone, a land line, civilian land line telephone. There was also a telephone used for extension. And there was" -- what else was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An induction telephone, a field telephone that the troops used when they go into field. It doesn't have a bell but a handle that is turned in order to start a call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you're referring to a telephone used for extension, are you referring to a military phone that's connected to a switchboard?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: We had a switchboard in the Standard barracks, and that switchboard was connected to extension lines, and those were connected to the telephones in the offices of the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to complete this thought, sir, when you refer to in the offices of the officers, are you referring to officers within the Zvornik Brigade or both in the Zvornik Brigade and outside of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Those extensions were in the offices of the officers of the Zvornik Brigade, but not only of the officers but also of everybody who was in the barracks of the Zvornik Brigade. In other words, those who were in the barracks could be connected via the extension lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would ask you to just take a few moments and explain to the Trial Chamber what the position of the operations duty officer entailed.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: An operations duty officer is tasked with registering every call that comes in, and also to register what is being said during such a telephone conversation. They have to register who called and who the called person was. If a message needs to be conveyed, then the duty operations officer conveys such a message to whomever is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you refer to every call that comes in, are you referring to both calls from within the brigade coming in as well as calls from outside the brigade coming in?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: All calls coming in and reaching operations duty officer. They are all registered, both from within the brigade and from outside the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to the task of registering every call. Did the duty officer maintain any written record or log of some kind of the phone calls and the subject matter of the calls as they came in during each shift?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: The calls were registered in the logbook of the operations duty officer, and those calls referred to the requirements in the battalions, the situation in the battalions, the development -- developments in the battalions. Those calls came from the information centre. All this came through the switchboard in the Standard barracks and reached the desk of the operations duty officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just one other question, sir, before I forget: You're familiar with the IKMs, or the forward command posts, of the brigade, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how would the Standard Brigade maintain contact with the IKMs?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: There were two types of connections. One was a wire connection, from the IKM to the switchboard in the brigade. That was a wire connection. Up there, they also had a field switchboard. This could also be used to establish communication. And if those lines were interrupted, there was also radio connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just back to the role and responsibility of the operations duty officer, how long was each shift for the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: A duty officer was on duty for 24 hours; however, it is impossible for one man to maintain that duty around the clock. That's why he is assigned an assistant, and the assistant is on duty while the duty operations officer is asleep, or if he has to go somewhere, then it is the assistant who takes his stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there, sir, a particular time period during which the assistant to the duty officer would typically work while the actual duty officer was sleeping?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Customarily, it was between midnight and until 6.00 or half of 6.00 the following morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think you alluded this -- to this already, sir, but during a given shift, who would physically be in the operations duty office?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Only and exclusively the operations duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you described the book in which these calls and the subject matter were recorded, but would the events of a previous shift be orally communicated to the brigade command each day?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: An operations duty officer has to brief the commander in the morning after the end of his duty, because if there is an urgent need for a battalion to be deployed, then a decision can be made -- made urgently. In other words, after the end of his shift, every morning the duty operations officer has to brief the commander of what had happened during his shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you refer to the commander, are you referring to the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from what level of the brigade's officers would the operations duty officers be drawn?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Operations duty officers were higher ranking officers that were billeted in the barracks of the Zvornik Brigade, in the Standard barracks, and I was on duty because I was the chief of communications. In other words, the chiefs of various branches, assistants for various duties, were assigned as operations duty officers. In other words, they are all higher-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, why was this position entrusted to these higher level officers as opposed to non-commissioned officers or lower level officers?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: In my view, because this was a highly sensitive duty that carried a lot of responsibilities and it had to be carried out responsibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, at this time, I'd ask that P00377 be brought up on e-court, and with Madam Usher's assistance I'd like to show you the -- well, I'll just show you an exhibit, the physical exhibit. This is not the document with the page hanging by a -- a hanging chad. Sir, I'd ask you just to take a look at the item that's before you, and, if you would, just flip through the pages and I would ask you if you recognise what that item is.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: This is the duty officer's -- duty operation officer's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we may turn to page 154 on e-court of the B/C/S, and that's page 35 of the English. Sir, you're going to see, I hope, an image on your screen in a moment. And if that's -- if we could scroll down to the bottom of the page, please, and sir, if it's easier for you to look at the original, there is a yellow sticky on the page that I believe is also that same page before you. But can you -- that's fine. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Usher. Okay. I see that you're -- you're looking at both the screen and the original document. Do you recognise your handwriting on this page that's before you?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I see at the bottom of the screen, below 005, my handwriting begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And would you please just read the first line of the text that you identify as being your handwriting, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: "Acquainted the commander of the R Battalion with the order."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is there a time that you've noted next to that entry, please?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: It says 0005.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I know you've been shown these pages and you've had an opportunity to review this document previously. Do you recall who was the duty officer during this shift that's captured here and on which you've made some entries?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I didn't remember because I didn't recognise the handwriting; however, when I gave my statement, they told me it was Trbic, because 12 years is a lot of time and I'm not good at identifying handwritings.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall what Mr. Trbic's position in the brigade was?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, he was assistant Chief of Staff for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may turn to the next page, that's page 155 of the B/C/S and page 36 of the English, and again, sir, do you see a new image on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I see half the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. If it's more legible for you to look at the original notebook, please feel free to do that. I just want to turn your attention to the entry for 0445 hours.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Duty operations officer called Zlatar, and I informed him that there had been no problems during the night, and "the situation is business as usual."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, what is your recollection as to what the term "Zlatar" refers to?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, Zlatar was the secret code name for the headquarters of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, as you sit here, do you recall what the code for the Main Staff was?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Vaguely, because code names changed, but I think it was Panorama.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall what the code for the Zvornik Brigade was?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I don't, honestly I don't. I seem to remember, in fact the word "Badem" springs to mind but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the entry that you just read, the call from, you recall, Zlatar, being the Drina Corps, was that typical of the types of contacts that were made from the outside into the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, situation was supposed to be reported on a regular basis, but if any problems occurred on the -- in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, they checked on the situation in brigades, just as the duty operations officer checked on the situation in battalions, because, you see, at 0500, "situation in battalions checked," it's business as usual, which means that I did check what the situation was in battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would look at the entry for 0535 hours, please? And just read that, if you can read what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: "Duty operations officer of Zlatar called. Trbic needs to call back."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would read the next entry, please? At 0540 hours.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: "At 5.40, Galic to call the chief at the forward command post. Completed." The chief was Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would please read the last entry that you have there on this page?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: "1st Infantry Battalion asks whether building machinery has been secured. Situation is normal. Trbic needs to call back."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I see a particular term that -- that you've written down in this entry, sir, and forgive me if I don't pronounce it well, but the word, "gradjevinski," can you tell the Trial Chamber in your experience what types of machines or machinery does that word refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: The call from the 1st Infantry Battalion did not specify which construction machinery was meant, but we understand that to mean excavators, bulldozers and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the entry, sir, at 0535 hours says, basically Trbic has to call, and the last entry more or less says, Trbic to report. Do these entries jog your memory at all about how you may have recalled that Trbic was the duty officer during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I object to that question because this witness has already said that he doesn't -- didn't remember who the duty officer was and that they told him who it was when he had the interview. Now, the Prosecutor hasn't gone further yet and asked who they are who told him it was Trbic, and I object to that question because he's already answered he didn't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I don't recall that being the testimony of the witness. I believe the witness said he wasn't sure, but that during the interview he told the OTP investigators that his recollection was Mr. Trbic, but I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that the discussion ought to continue in the presence of the witness in the first place. That's number 1. Secondly, let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Court, you might look at the page 62, the answer starting at line 2, 3, and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, my learned friend is correct. I misrecollected the testimony, Your Honours. I think the question is still a fair question to find out whether this is consistent with his recollection that he -- or with what he's testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't believe that's fair at all by Mr. Thayer. It's very clear that the witness said he didn't remember, he had no recollection, he didn't recall the handwriting, and that "they told me it was Trbic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. But the question that Mr. Thayer is trying to put now is somewhat different, given what you have already stated, given what the witness himself has already stated, now he's being referred specifically to this entry and he is being asked whether this helps him in any way to jog his memory. In other words, does he still remain the same position as he was before and referred to the duty officer upon the suggestion of the Prosecution, or does now this entry help him to jog his memory and tell us whether now he remembers. This is basically the difference between the previous question and statement and answer and the present one. So go ahead. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Judge, Your Honour, with all due respect, I believe Mr. Thayer is misleading the Court, especially at page 64, lines 19 through 22, where he says I don't believe the witness said that he wasn't sure but during that interview he told the OTP investigator that his recollection was Trbic when in fact the witness has already said he didn't recall and that they told me. I don't know if they want to mislead you that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. This is -- I would temper a little bit the language that you tend to use sometimes, Mr. Meek because when you use such language, you are attributing bad faith to Mr. Thayer, and I would seriously object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I certainly attribute bad faith to Mr. Thayer if he simply said he made a mistake, but if you read the record, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Sit down, Mr. Meek. Go ahead and repeat your question, Mr. Thayer, or rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, the entry at 0535 hours says that Trbic has to call, and the last entry you read refers to Trbic having to report. My question is: Having read these two entries, does that jog your memory at all about who the duty officer was on this shift or are you still at the point where the only recollection you have of Mr. Trbic being the duty officer was what the OTP told you during your interview? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, after all my talks with the investigators, I remembered it was Trbic. But the first entry saying he should report means he should report to the duty officer of the Zlatar, and the second entry means he should report or rather call back the brigade. There were two different addresses [as interpreted] that he was supposed to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's make this clear. There was one stage where you were still uncertain in your mind as to who the duty officer was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I talked to the investigator, when he showed me the handwriting and asked whose handwriting it was, I said I don't remember. And then when he said it was Trbic's handwriting, then I remembered that I was Trbic's assistant that evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we -- may we look at the next page of this document, that's page 37 of the English and page 156 of the B/C/S, please? Sir, do you see a new image if front of you on the computer?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you see a date that's written in the upper right-hand corner, and, if you do, can you just read what it is into the record?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: "17th July 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether there was any procedure regarding how the date of each shift was to be recorded in this notebook or logbook?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of a shift, the date should be written, and every duty operations officer when he begins he writes the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So in your experience, this entry, July 17th, 1995, was entered at the beginning of the shift on the day of -- sometime on the day of July 17th, 1995; is that -- am I understanding you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, based on the hours that you testified that you would typically work as the assistant to the operations duty officer, that is from midnight to 6.00 in the morning, is what you're telling us that you wouldn't write down the date necessarily at 12.01 in the morning of July 17th you would wait a few or a few hours would pass, and then the actual duty officer who came on duty would make an entry at the point where the duty officer came on later in the morning? And if that question made no sense to you, please just let me know and I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: The question is clear. It was not the practice when you finish a shift -- I mean it was the practice when you finish a shift, you would turn over the duty, and my shift obviously finished around 6.00 because you don't see any more of my handwriting. The person who took over wrote the date and started making his own entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So based on the date that's shown on this page, can you just tell the Trial Chamber what date it was when Mr. Trbic first started his duty?

utterances.speaker: MILANKO JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, Trbic took over on that day when I was his assistant. It should be the 16th, although I don't see it here. When I finished my shift, and he took over, he continued to make entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I don't think I have any further questions for you right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Thayer. I have several of the Defence teams that wish to cross-examine this witness. Who is going first? We have got ten minutes or just less than ten minutes. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will not cross-examine this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Given the time and the fact that we are going to be visiting with our client, I would like to start tomorrow with what I've heard today on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Is there anyone who can cross-examine this witness in eight minutes? None. Let's go through the list again. The Nikolic team, will you be cross-examining this witness? Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Borovcanin, you've said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, we will not cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. More or less, you know where you stand. I think we need to stop here today. Agreed? Agreed? And you need to have the next witness prepared for tomorrow because I reckon we will be less than one hour with this witness tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He's ready to go, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we stand adjourned, to tomorrow, 9.00. Now, Witness, before you leave this courtroom, as you see, we haven't finished with your testimony today. We'll finish tomorrow. But between today and tomorrow, it's important that you do not communicate with anyone on the matters that you are testifying upon. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
